reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard haematology references
clinicalPearls: A form of autoimmune haemolytic anaemia mediated by IgM autoantibodies that bind red cells maximally at low temperatures
Because IgM fixes complement efficiently, haemolysis is predominantly complement-mediated and largely extravascular in the liver, with intravascular haemolysis in severe cases
Cold exposure provokes acrocyanosis and Raynaud-like symptoms of the extremities, ears and nose as red cells agglutinate in cooler peripheral vessels
Primary (chronic) cold agglutinin disease is associated with an underlying clonal low-grade B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder in the marrow
Secondary cold agglutinin syndrome follows infections, classically Mycoplasma pneumoniae (anti-I) and infectious mononucleosis (anti-i), and less commonly lymphoma
The direct antiglobulin test is positive for complement (C3d) and negative or weak for IgG, and blood films and analysers may show red cell agglutination that corrects on warming

Management principles centre on keeping the patient warm and avoiding cold, with treatment of any underlying infection or lymphoproliferative disorder; B-cell directed therapy and complement inhibition are used in significant disease
Corticosteroids and splenectomy are generally ineffective, in contrast to warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
Laboratory samples must be kept warm to avoid spurious agglutination and inaccurate counts
reference.pathophysiology: Cold agglutinin disease is caused by IgM autoantibodies, usually directed against the I antigen on red cells, that bind optimally at temperatures below core body temperature. In the cooler peripheral circulation the antibody binds red cells and activates the classical complement pathway, depositing C3b; as cells return to the warm central circulation the antibody dissociates but complement-coated cells are cleared, predominantly by hepatic macrophages (extravascular haemolysis), with intravascular haemolysis when complement activation is intense. Agglutination of red cells in cool vessels produces the circulatory symptoms. Primary disease reflects a clonal B-cell lymphoproliferative process producing monoclonal cold agglutinin, whereas secondary forms follow infection or lymphoma with polyclonal or transient antibody.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of haemolysis (microangiopathic, drug-induced, hereditary)
Cryoglobulinaemia and other cold-related vascular phenomena
additionalInvestigations: Direct antiglobulin test showing C3d positivity with negative or weak IgG
Cold agglutinin titre and thermal amplitude
Blood film for red cell agglutination and haemolysis markers (LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin, reticulocytes)
Serum protein electrophoresis, immunoglobulins and marrow evaluation for a lymphoproliferative disorder
Screening for Mycoplasma and Epstein-Barr virus in acute secondary cases
redFlags: Severe acute haemolysis with rapidly falling haemoglobin
Haemoglobinuria and features of intravascular haemolysis
Underlying lymphoma or lymphoproliferative disorder identified on workup
Peripheral ischaemia or acrocyanosis progressing to tissue compromise
reference.prognosis: Primary cold agglutinin disease is usually a chronic condition with variable haemolysis; many patients do well with cold avoidance, but significant disease can cause disabling symptoms and anaemia, and outcome is influenced by the underlying clonal disorder. Post-infectious secondary forms are typically transient and resolve with recovery from the infection.
pitfalls: Relying on corticosteroids or splenectomy, which are largely ineffective in cold agglutinin disease
Failing to keep blood samples warm, producing spurious agglutination and inaccurate red cell indices
Missing an underlying B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder in chronic primary disease
Transfusing cold blood or infusing cold fluids and worsening haemolysis
Confusing it with warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and choosing the wrong therapy
